summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity. It stands under the French national framework: France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents, the justice system and the prison service, while the collectivity legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are French national provisions, applying here because French law governs.

France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of transgender detainees' rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty, a finding that by its terms covers establishments here. Its referrals since 2010 covered some forty transgender persons, and its on-site inspections at four establishments in France interviewed eight trans women and one trans man; no inspection of a New Caledonian establishment is documented.

Under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, trans women in French prisons are placed according to their legal gender marker rather than anatomy, which in practice means all-male facilities where they face threats of assault by other detainees; a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 documented this pattern, and the French prison framework applies to this collectivity's establishments as French law.

Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality law, signed 18 May 2013, under which a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry here. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on France's first same-sex wedding under that law; PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012.

The inventory records no New Caledonia-specific law, enforcement action, incident, institution or statistic bearing on trans visitors, and no local ordinance narrowing the national protections. No region-specific signal was identified beyond the extension of the French framework, and the national assessment for France applies.
tangentialFactors:
Discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code in July 2012, enabling prosecution of discrimination and transphobia as discrimination; the wording was updated to "gender identity" on 18 November 2016. French law applies to the collectivity.

Transgender people in France can change legal gender without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical diagnosis under the law signed 18 November 2016 following a 17 November Constitutional Council ruling, effective 1 January 2017, though a court appearance is still required; first-name change can be done at a registry office. France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, the first country to declassify gender dysphoria, though transgender organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale and in-country gender-affirming surgery legalised since 1979.

Since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by imprisonment, and conversion therapy was banned by a law passed by the Senate 7 December 2020, concurred by the National Assembly 25 January 2022 and published 1 February 2022, following a 2019 proposal for two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine.

A 2022 ILGA-Europe report on care in France found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location, and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine characterised increased demand as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and "primarily social problem" advising extreme caution without changing practice, and late-2024 pediatric guidelines recommend puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D.

A Senate bill passed in May 2024 to ban medical transition under age 18 followed a March 2024 Little Mermaid Observatory report calling such care a health scandal, but it has had no update since 23 July 2024, is opposed by the Macron government and is unlikely to pass the Assembly amid large protests. In 2022 the DILCRAH scientific committee president was revealed as a member of the Observatory, which called care "mutilation," leading to one committee resignation.

Police in France recorded around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018, after President Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as unworthy of France. This is a France-wide figure combining homophobic and transphobic attacks, not a New Caledonia-specific or trans-only count, and no denominator or population context is given.
localsOnly:
Residents of New Caledonia stand under the French Labour Code bar on exclusion from recruitment, sanction, dismissal or other discriminatory measures on the ground of gender identity, and under the Penal Code ground of discrimination on that wording since 18 November 2016, previously drafted as sexual identity from July 2012.

Transphobic motive has been an aggravating factor for crimes punishable by imprisonment since 2017, and the conversion-therapy ban published 1 February 2022 applies. Detainees are placed by legal gender marker rather than anatomy under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code.

National legislation since 1985 prohibits sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments with a maximum €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité, amended the 29 July 1881 Press Law, and increases penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in New Caledonia under the law signed 18 May 2013 after a 17 May 2013 constitutional ruling, following registered PACS partnerships since 1999.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the CGLPL's 25 May 2021 finding on serious violations of transgender detainees' rights has been acted on in New Caledonian establishments is unresolved: no inspection of a New Caledonian establishment is documented in this record, and no post-2021 follow-up covering the collectivity is sourced.

The BuzzFeed News account of trans women held in all-male facilities facing assault threats is a France-wide feature of 12 January 2018; its incidence in New Caledonian prisons specifically is not sourced here.

The 1,870-victim police figure for 2019 combines homophobic and transphobic attacks across France with no trans-only breakdown and no population denominator; its application to New Caledonia is not sourced.

The status of the May 2024 Senate bill on medical transition under age 18 is unresolved beyond its last documented update of 23 July 2024; no later outcome is sourced.

Whether any local New Caledonian ordinance addresses conversion therapy, detention placement or gender-marker changes beyond the French framework is not sourced in this inventory.
